quote: Suche den Fundamentalsatz der projektiven Ge- ometrie (Wenn [-die 2-] 2 Dreiecke so liegen, dass die 3 Paare entsprechender Seiten sich auf der nämlichen Geraden schneiden, so laufen die 3 durch [-die-] entsprechende Ecken gelegten Geraden durch einen Punkt), ohne aus der Ebene herauszutreten, zu beweisen oder suche den Nachweis zu führen, dass dies unmöglich ist.
english: Try to prove the fundamental theorem of projective geometry (if 2 triangles are situated so that the 3 pairs of corresponding sides intersect on the same line, then the 3 lines drawn through corresponding vertices pass through one point) without leaving the plane, or try to show that this is impossible.
topic: Hilbert sets the task of proving Desargues' theorem without leaving the plane, or showing this is impossible, and then sketches an abstract incidence-style correspondence between two (in space, three) sorts of objects, such as points and lines, on whose relations all of synthetic geometry rests.

triage.modern_statement: Take a projective plane defined only by the plane incidence axioms (any two points lie on a unique line, any two lines meet, plus non-degeneracy). Is Desargues' theorem a consequence of these axioms? Hilbert writes it in the dual form: two triangles perspective from a line are perspective from a point. Either prove it from plane axioms alone, without using points outside the plane or a third dimension, or show that no such proof exists. In model-theoretic terms: is there a non-Desarguesian plane, meaning a model of the plane axioms in which the Desargues configuration fails? A refinement Hilbert also handled: Desargues holds in a plane exactly when that plane can be embedded in a higher-dimensional geometry, and equivalently, in modern terms, when it can be coordinatized over a division ring.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert himself, in Grundlagen der Geometrie (Festschrift for the Gauss–Weber celebration, 1899), Chapter V. He built a plane geometry that satisfies all the linear and plane axioms (incidence I1–2, order, parallels, continuity and congruence IV1–5) but not congruence axiom IV6, and in which Desargues' theorem fails. So the theorem cannot be proved in the plane without the space axioms or full congruence. He also showed that a plane satisfying his plane axioms can be embedded in a higher-dimensional geometry if and only if Desargues holds in it. F. R. Moulton gave a simpler non-Desarguesian plane (the Moulton plane) in Trans. AMS 3 (1902), 192–195.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899), Chapter V, states that there is a plane geometry satisfying axioms I1–2, II–III, IV1–5 and V (all linear and plane axioms except congruence axiom IV6) in which Desargues' theorem does not hold.

Moulton (1902) cites Hilbert's 1899 Grundlagen, Chapter V: a plane geometry satisfying the plane axioms can be part of a spatial geometry of more than two dimensions exactly when Desargues' theorem holds in it. Moulton then gives a simpler non-Desarguesian plane.
Encyclopedia of Mathematics: Desargues's theorem cannot be proved in the plane from the projective plane axioms alone, without the congruence (metric) axioms or the space axioms.
AMS Notices: the observation that Desargues' theorem can fail in projective planes, and the term 'non-Desarguesian', go back to Hilbert.

triage.why: This diary entry poses the problem that Hilbert answered in the negative in Chapter V of the 1899 Grundlagen: a non-Desarguesian plane exists, so a proof that stays in the plane is impossible. Moulton's 1902 example confirmed this more simply. The question is not among the 23 Paris problems. It is the classic starting point of the theory of non-Desarguesian planes. That theory is still studied, for example in finite geometry and the classification of non-Desarguesian planes, but the question as posed here has been settled for a long time. One caveat: the formulation in the note is the converse (dual) form of Desargues. In the projective setting this form is equivalent to the usual one, so the same answer applies.
